Mixing close-range action freneticism with a gorgeous, meditative atmosphere, Beast of Reincarnation is fun, admirable, gorgeous and flawed.

What is it? A melancholy parry-happy action RPG from the creators of Pokémon games Release date August 4, 2026 Expect to pay $60 Developer Game Freak Publisher Fictions Reviewed on RTX 3060 (laptop), Ryzen 5 5600H, 16GB RAM Steam Deck Unsupported Link Steam

Beast of Reincarnation is a sci-fi action RPG whose parry-happy woman protagonist is on a mission to save an apocalypse-blighted humanity. On paper it sounds like Stellar Blade , and in practice, it feels a bit like Stellar Blade. It's open but linear, and ruthlessly focused on speed and dexterity. And yet, while Beast of Reincarnation may draw from the same pool of inspiration—think Sekiro , Final Fantasy , Nier —the net result is cosmically at odds with Shift Up's outing.

Emma is a young woman stricken by the Blight. It's the very same phenomenon that has transformed 41st century Japan into a wasteland of verdant ruins. She entirely lacks emotion thanks to her malady, nor can she remember her life before the illness. To make matters worse, she's an outcast among survivors by dint of her condition. But in exchange she has inherited some gnarly Blight powers, namely the ability to generate aggressive, tentacle-like flora.

The Blight is an infection spread by the titular beast of reincarnation, whose wrath is renewed every hundred years. Though an outcast, Emma and her similarly Blight-infected dog companion Koo are tasked with taking the fight to this mysterious deity-like beast. So off they go, chaperoned by a small crew in a giant military biped which serves as home base.

The flagrantly unoriginal premise seems to promise a bombastic, relentlessly loud spectacle. But entirely to its credit, Beast of Reincarnation is an unusually quiet and patient thing. If Stellar Blade is psytrance with the bass jacked right up, Beast of Reincarnation is psytrance with the percussion removed entirely. I mean, it's essentially a precision-oriented action game, and it can often be very tense, but the whole project is suffused with an elegiac doom. This is a richly atmospheric, melancholy videogame. It took me by surprise.

reviews.title: Beast of Reincarnation Review: Boring World, Beguiling Combat
reviews.identity_evidence: Direct registered professional publisher review verified for Beast of Reincarnation.
evidence_points: Emma, a mysterious old man named Brad, a young girl named Kagura, and your trusty wolf companion Koo travel throughout Japanese colonies in a Cleanse Walker mech. Emma, a purifier, is tasked with, well, purifying beasts overtaken by a blight en route to the Capitol, where she must defeat the Beast of Reincarnation to save mankind.

These characters talk directly to Beast of Reincarnation’s transparent themes, taking a blunt approach and leaving little for the player to dissect or work through. The importance of friendship, family, having a soul, fighting to save people, and more are discussed ad nauseum in overly long cutscenes void of life. These characters are paper-thin, and the story, which features predictable arcs, lackluster villains, and plot beats about Koo you’ve seen in dozens of other dog-related stories, does little to inspire me as the controller of Emma. But her blade picks up the slack.

Game Freak blends Emma’s Sekiro- and Stellar Blade-style swordplay, which relies on parrying, dodging, and stagger bars, with Koo’s QTE elemental abilities that are reminiscent of last year’s Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 to create an excellent combat system. So excellent, in fact, that sitting through 10-plus-minute cutscenes after each milestone of progression is doubly excruciating. For a game that demonstrates such confidence in its combat, Game Freak is determined to pull you away from it with yet another exposition dump.

While clearly pulling from the aforementioned inspirations, Beast of Reincarnation’s combat is easier. Bosses and more elite enemies still pose a great challenge, but generous HP recovery, powerful attacks that are easy to pull off, and large parry and dodge windows will help the less experienced feel capable and seasoned players feel untouchable.

Initially, boss fights are tense arenas for learning and mastering the combat. However, they, too, become repetitive, with recurring bosses appearing far too much, especially for what are meant to be Beast of Reincarnation’s end-of-stage setpiece moments. Pay attention too closely, and you’ll find that enemies share many animations, removing the enigma of duels and bouts. It doesn’t help that Beast of Reincarnation takes a formulaic approach to each stage, either: The big boss of the area appears for a quick fight at the start, runs off when you’ve hurt it enough, and then waits in its lair while you fight through the stage until you reach it for a proper fight. But still, fighting a boss, whether a repeat or not, means engaging in the game’s combat, and doing so is congenial throughout.

Challenge aside, which comes in three difficulty settings, the combat is rewarding and highly reflexive to one’s strengths. I stuck to an elemental build where I’d begin each fight with Koo’s lightning Javelin equipped with a 2x status build-up mod, allowing my lightning-imbued katana to inflict the “Shock” effect in just seconds. That creates a window of paralysis that lets Emma’s various combo moves and finishers inflict heavy damage and stagger, if not outright kill.

And that’s just one of the many builds I experimented with in Beast of Reincarnation. There’s room for ranged, stealth, fire, poison builds, and more. Through an expansive skill tree that continues to grow, even after the game’s final (and anticlimactic) fight, there’s no world where two players’ Emmas work the same. Generous attribute points used for raising attack, defense, and the usual standard RPG stats make the act of doing so feel inconsequential, and I rarely paid attention to my progression here. But the subsequent skill points I’d unlock, which let me power up specific abilities and moves in Emma and Koo’s kit, came in the dozens, and working through the associated skill tree was a gluttonous climb of power.

There’s a unique double jump in the form of a vine that Emma can use to push herself higher, and she can use those vines to whip to high-up perches and locations, but Game Freak is uninterested in how this might affect locomotion outside of battle. Utilizing these vines to get some air and slam down into enemies below with my Helm-Splitter ability is a treat – whipping up to a boring hallway littered with boring enemies to open a boring chest with boring rewards inside is not.

You will open the same type of chest to receive the same types of resources countless times, and the “take all” button is your best friend because what these items do matters little. There are crops to grow from seedlings collected for Kagura to cook up stat-boosting meals, but these bonuses are negligible. There are skulls to collect to power up your Cleanse Walker, but I had maxed out this mech before the game’s halfway point. There are books (you can’t read) to collect, rations for a hunger system that matters little, and currency you will never struggle to accumulate. Seeking out these resources is as rote as the resources themselves.

The final act of Beast of Reincarnation, with its telegraphed revelations and color-by-numbers moments, left me feeling… nothing. But the ensuing New Game+ notification stopped me from uninstalling the game after the credits rolled. I don’t know if I’ll return to play more, but if I do, it won’t be because of Emma, but rather, what Emma’s sword can do.

Beast of Reincarnation is a great ARPG, with firm but fair combat and wide scope for crafting a build to your tastes. Surprisingly, perhaps, it also has a deep and thoughtful story that it trusts you to dig into yourself. Let Game Freak henceforth be known as the Beast of Reincarnation studio.

With a name like Beast of Reincarnation you might expect this to be a game full of aggressive enemies and intense combat. And it is. Yet it's not long before you start to discover that there are layers to this world, and the people who live in it. Layers that make this a strong and deep experience rather than a fun but shallow action game.

Don't get me wrong; there is a lot of fighting. That's almost exclusively what you'll be doing, and in fact, I found it greatly amusing that I came across a grand total of one puzzle in my playthrough. You take the role of Emma, a young woman who is tasked with killing the titular Beast, the source of post-apocalyptic Japan's Blight that mutates animals, spreads pretty but corrupted foliage, and kills people. Before she can do so however, she'll need to kill many of the giant creatures known as Nushi in order to absorb their power, and cleanse the surrounding areas as she buffs up. There's no shortage of lesser enemies standing between her and each Nushi, either.
Release date: August 4, 2026 Platform(s): PC, PS5, Xbox Series X Developer: Game Freak Publisher: Fictions

Please don't mistake Beast of Reincarnation, with its high-fidelity sci-fi, and sword-wielding, reserved heroine for being much like Stellar Blade. Unlike that game's star Eve, who is uncomfortably thrust into danger in form-fitting bodysuits that leave nothing to the imagination, Emma is dressed like an actual fighter who takes her job seriously. She also behaves like an actual, real character – unlike many similar heroes, her aloofness has a specific reason behind it which is slowly revealed. She even experiences character growth.

It's a good thing Emma's well armored too. Beast of Reincarnation has combat that is challenging from a very early stage. I was tempted to knock the difficulty down within the first hour or so, in fact – and if that works best for you, it's a perfectly good way to enjoy this or any other game – but, in my case, I'm glad that I didn't. There's a real sense of satisfaction to be had emerging from a tough fight battered, low on resources, close to death – but alive.

reviews.identity_evidence: Direct registered professional publisher review verified for Beast of Reincarnation.
evidence_points: Beast of Reincarnation presents itself like a Souls-like action RPG, and it definitely shares some traits with games of that ilk, but I think labelling it that way isn't quite accurate.

It is an action RPG, but it's not as intimidatingly difficult as FromSoftware's efforts, and it's doing enough stuff of its own that makes it much more interesting than yet another copycat of that formula.
That being said, the game's influences are clear, but it melds elements together in a way that mostly works very well.

You play as Emma, a woman cursed by a plant-based blight that robs her of human emotion but grants her extraordinary abilities. She exists in a post-apocalyptic Japan, one reclaimed by nature and infested with dangerous plant-animal hybrids called malefacts.
Having bonded with one such creature, a large wolf named Koo, it's down to the pair to rid the world of the titular Beast of Reincarnation and save the remainder of humanity.
What that means for the player is a pretty simply structured action adventure. You explore a series of open zones and must defeat the Nushi — the boss — that presides over each one.
Each map is reasonably big and allows you to run around freely. When you're ready, you can follow the main objective to pursue the boss, progress the story, and move onto the next area.

Some maps feel more open than others, but I enjoyed this aspect of the world design. You're given a lot of reasons to poke around; there are optional mini-bosses and lots of useful, valuable items to discover away from the golden path.
The environmental design is also pretty nice for the most part. Whether it's grasslands and ruined villages or a massive underground settlement, there are some interesting sights to behold as you go.
Sometimes they can feel a little dull to move through, as there isn't a lot of dynamic stuff happening outside of battles.

reviews.title: Beast of Reincarnation Review | TheSixthAxis
reviews.identity_evidence: Direct registered professional publisher review verified for Beast of Reincarnation.
evidence_points: Beast of Reincarnation draws a quiet and sombre picture of the fall of mankind. Civilisation fell 1000 years ago, and what’s left is truly the dregs at the bottom of the barrel. The world has been corrupted by the blight, all stemming forth from the titular Beast of Reincarnation. Every 100 years, the beast rises again, bringing further chaos and destruction to a dwindling population that already have next to nothing. It’s bleak.

That’s where our heroine Emma comes in. She’s a purifier, sent out to battle the blight and its hosts of infected creatures and golem. She doesn’t make for a typical protagonist, though, loathed by the general populace for her own blight infection, which in turn has robbed her of all emotion and care. She is, in many ways, an empty vessel, but one which you will see to filling through the course of the story.

The first step on that road is Koo, a large malefact that takes the form of a dog. He too is infected by the blight, but after Emma saves him from a critical wound, they form an inseparable bond, one that’s punctuated by cuddles, a wondrously floofy coat, and the times where Emma showers with the giant dog to remove the blood of their enemies. Yes, really.

Emma’s life is pretty messed up. She’s an outcast, thanks to her infection from the blight, with the few remaining humans shunning her, treating her like dirt, and calling her “stained”. The golem aren’t much better, at least the ones that oversee the towns and settlements, and she’s fitted with a toxic choker that will kill her if she steps out of line. She’s clearly seen as a tool, a necessary evil, who’s called upon to deal with the blight, the immense Nushi, or infected golem, and despite all this, she answers the call.

Much of the story and character progression centres around Emma and her small entourage, who see her as a person, beyond the blight that’s tangled throughout her body. Emma is without emotion, often struggling to understand the social cues, needs and desires of those around her, and while this could have come off as robotic and distant, it’s actually quite touching and gently dealt with, expanding on the underlying threads of loneliness and reflecting the damaged and largely empty world she inhabits. It’s distinctly Japanese, and that might not sit comfortably with western audiences.

Beast of Reincarnation strikes a melancholic tone, a quietude that carries a surprising amount of depth and emotion. There’s Emma, detached and unsure how to interact with the world, while carrying a deep sense of loss, both for her own humanity and for those around her. That loss extends out into the world, its shattered and ruined remains speaking to what we have now, and extrapolating a course where humanity is at the brink of extinction.

It’s increasingly cinematic, though it feels more like a high-concept sci-fi indie than a Disney-fied blockbuster. I loved the plaintive soundtrack, the detached protagonist, and the design of post-apocalyptic Japan, decaying buildings given over to the blight, with an early highlight being the way the forest rises up and changes the landscape with the arrival of the Nushi.

The Nushi are gigantic boss creatures that punctuate the end of each area, and they’re very close in design and feel to the naturalistic monsters of EA’s monster-hunting Wild Hearts . The tendrils of vines, flowering branches and unnatural growths that flow through and across each Nushi are so reminiscent that you could interchange them between either game, though that’s not to diminish the fact that they still look and feel distinctive enough to stand alone.

Beast of Reincarnation is fundamentally a Souls-lite, taking a number of crucial elements from the genre and reducing the difficulty somewhat. That’s not to say it’s easy, because it’s not. If you find yourself surrounded, or mistime a few parries, you’ll need to prepare for a swift and ignominious death. Growth, combat abilities and upgrades come quickly though, and you retain any skill points earned before you died, making it a much smoother and less frustrating path, even if the need to grind remains.

There’s not the widest variety of enemies, but some of them are so lethal, and their silhouette so distinct, that you’ll still get a rush of adrenaline when you decide to face them, rather than skirt around them, and carry on with your day.
